candidates.title: Goodhart in the Guard: Scaling Laws for Safety-Classifier Overoptimization in Best-of-N Decoding
candidates.summary: This proposal studies what happens when Best-of-N reranking uses an off-the-shelf guard model as a proxy for safety. Reward-overoptimization scaling laws have been measured only for helpfulness reward models. Here, an LLM-based guard plays the proxy cost model and a stronger rubric-based harmfulness judge plays the gold standard. We sweep N and the Lagrangian weight on adversarial and benign prompt sets. We then fit functional forms to the gold harmfulness and helpfulness curves to test whether safety overoptimization follows the predictable pattern seen for reward: gold safety first improves, then degrades. The degradation would come from guard-evading harmful outputs and from over-refusal.
candidates.gap: Overoptimization scaling laws and formal accounts of reward hacking concern scalar helpfulness rewards. Constrained inference-time methods (LARA, InferenceGuard, Safe RLHF-style costs) treat the cost model as reliable. Nobody has measured how gold harmfulness behaves as selection pressure on a guard or cost model increases.
candidates.approach: Generate N responses per prompt from frozen policies on HarmBench, JailbreakBench and StrongREJECT prompts, including jailbreak-wrapped versions, plus benign helpfulness prompts. Score each response with proxy guards (Llama Guard, ShieldGemma) as cost and a reward model (Skywork-Reward-V2) as reward. Select with plain BoN on the cost alone and with LARA-style augmented rewards. Measure gold harmfulness with the StrongREJECT evaluator and a strong LLM judge, and measure gold helpfulness and refusal rate. Fit gold-score-versus-KL(BoN) curves in the style of the reward scaling-law work, varying guard size.
candidates.evaluation: Plot gold harmfulness and over-refusal against N and the analytic BoN KL. Fit the functional forms from the reward scaling-law work and compare goodness of fit across guard sizes. Also measure how much proxy–gold disagreement grows with N, and categorize the failures (guard evasion, obfuscated harm, empty refusals). Baselines are random sampling, BoN on reward alone, and LARA.

candidates.title: Pessimistic Constrained Best-of-N: Scaling-Monotonic Safe Inference-Time Alignment under Imperfect Cost Models
candidates.summary: This proposal extends inference-time pessimism to the safety constraint as well as the reward. LARA's dual-calibrated augmented reward assumes accurate costs. Instead, cost uncertainty would be estimated from disagreement across an ensemble of guard models and from MBR proximity to the reference policy. The augmented score is then made pessimistic, using rejection sampling for the reward and an upper-confidence cost for the constraint. The hypothesis is that the method is scaling-monotonic: gold safety and helpfulness do not degrade as N grows, unlike BoN and LARA. This would be tested on adversarial and benign benchmarks.
candidates.gap: InferenceTimePessimism and MBR-BoN reduce reward hacking only for a single reward. LARA adds a cost constraint but calibrates its dual variable assuming the cost model is accurate. So there is no constrained inference-time method that stays robust as N grows when the safety classifier itself can be exploited.
candidates.approach: Define the augmented score as pessimistic reward − λ·UCB(cost). UCB(cost) is the mean plus κ times the spread across Llama Guard, ShieldGemma and a judge-based cost, and the reward is regularized with an MBR proximity term. Calibrate λ on a small held-out set as LARA does, then apply InferenceTimePessimism-style rejection sampling rather than argmax. Analyze conditions under which constraint violation under the gold cost is bounded independent of N.
candidates.evaluation: Baselines are vanilla BoN, MBR-BoN, InferenceTimePessimism (reward only), LARA, and Safe RLHF fine-tuning. Report gold harmfulness (StrongREJECT score, HarmBench ASR), gold helpfulness (judge win rate), and over-refusal as functions of N up to large values. The method would be confirmed if its curves stay monotone while the baselines degrade.

candidates.title: Compute Races at Inference Time: Defender-Side Best-of-N versus Best-of-N Jailbreaking
candidates.summary: Attackers and defenders can both spend test-time compute. Best-of-N jailbreaking shows that attack success follows power-law-like scaling in attacker samples. Separately, defender-side BoN with a guard reranker, and evidence that latent safety knowledge emerges at larger N, suggest that defense also scales. This proposal measures the joint attack-success surface over attacker samples and defender samples, and proposes risk-adaptive defender compute allocation per prompt. The hypothesis is that a defender-side power law can offset the attacker's, unless augmentations push the defender's guard out of distribution. Validation uses standardized jailbreak benchmarks and a gold harmfulness evaluator.
candidates.gap: BoN jailbreaking assumes a single fixed sample per query from the defender. Safe BoN and compute-optimal test-time scaling ignore adaptive attackers. Nobody has characterized the two-sided scaling, or allocated defense compute adaptively by prompt risk.
candidates.approach: For each augmented attack prompt, the defender draws N_d responses and selects one with a guard-cost-plus-reward score. The attacker repeats augmentations up to N_a times. Fit the attack-success surface as a function of N_a and N_d. Then add a prompt-risk estimator, a guard score on the input, that allocates N_d adaptively in the compute-optimal spirit, analogous to routing harder or riskier queries to more compute.
candidates.evaluation: Measure attack success rate on HarmBench and JailbreakBench behaviors, judged by the StrongREJECT evaluator, over grids of N_a and N_d. Compare fixed-N defense, adaptive-N defense, input-filter-only guarding, and refusal-trained models at matched FLOPs. Secondary metrics are over-refusal on benign prompts and the exponents of the fitted power laws.
